Bang-bang CDR: turning the ISF's σ_t into K_bb, JTOL and SSC tracking

Prerequisites: serdes_clocking_connection (the loop high-pass intuition of §6, UI/eye/BER), pll_noise_budget (∣Hlp∣2,∣Hhp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2,\lvert H_{hp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2,∣Hhp​∣2, the jitter-transfer vs jitter-tolerance distinction and the JTOL worked example — reused directly here), dj_dual_dirac (Q−1(10−12)=7.03Q^{-1}(10^{-12})=7.03Q−1(10−12)=7.03, TJ@BER) | Next: exercises, lab_13_pll_cdr_transfer

serdes_clocking_connection drew the CDR (clock and data recovery) as a black box that "high-passes VCO noise and low-passes input jitter." A real SerDes receiver is almost never that linear PLL: it is a bang-bang (binary, "early/late" only) digital loop whose phase detector (PD) emits only ±1\pm1±1 and whose clock phase is moved by a phase interpolator (PI) in discrete steps of UI/2b\text{UI}/2^bUI/2b. This page answers three questions designers meet daily that none of the earlier pages answered:

  1. A bang-bang PD has no "gain" — so what sets the loop bandwidth? The answer: the rms value of the jitter, which is exactly the σt\sigma_tσt​ this site has been computing all along. Here the ISF sets not only the noise but the loop dynamics.
  2. Where does the datasheet jitter-tolerance mask (JTOL) — that broken line of "−40-40−40 dB/dec at low frequency, −20-20−20 dB/dec in the middle, a plateau at high frequency" — come from?
  3. SSC (spread-spectrum clocking) is a huge, deterministic low-frequency phase excursion the CDR must track: how large, and why a first-order loop cannot follow it.

Physical intuition (conclusion first): a bang-bang PD is a comparator; the slope of sign(Δt)\text{sign}(\Delta t)sign(Δt) versus Δt\Delta tΔt is infinite at 0 — but with noise present, the expected output E[sign(Δt+n)]E[\text{sign}(\Delta t+n)]E[sign(Δt+n)] is "smeared" into an error function whose slope is the finite 2/π/σj\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sigma_j2/π​/σj​. More noise, less gain, slower loop: this is a loop whose bandwidth scales itself with the jitter. JTOL is "how much eye margin is left" divided by "the fraction the loop fails to track, ∣1−H∣\lvert1-H\rvert∣1−H∣"; the triangular FM of SSC integrates to a parabolic phase of several hundred UI, and only a type-II loop with a frequency integrator can track it down to a few tenths of a UI.

Step 1: the Alexander (bang-bang) phase detector outputs sign(Δt)​

The Alexander PD (external literature, not among this site's five PDFs: J. D. H. Alexander, Electron. Lett., vol. 11, no. 22, pp. 541–542, Oct. 1975) decides whether the clock is early or late relative to the data edge from three samples: the two bit-center samples Dk−1,DkD_{k-1}, D_kDk−1​,Dk​ and, between them, the edge sample EkE_kEk​ nominally aligned with the data transition. The whole decision rests on one sentence: if the edge sampler fires before the data transition it still sees the old bit; if it fires after the transition it already sees the new bit.

  • Clock early: EkE_kEk​ falls before the transition and still sees the old bit → Ek=Dk−1≠DkE_k=D_{k-1}\ne D_kEk​=Dk−1​=Dk​.
  • Clock late: EkE_kEk​ falls after the transition and already sees the new bit → Ek=Dk≠Dk−1E_k=D_k\ne D_{k-1}Ek​=Dk​=Dk−1​.
  • Dk−1=DkD_{k-1}=D_kDk−1​=Dk​ (no transition) → no information, no output.
Dk−1D_{k-1}Dk−1​EkE_kEk​DkD_kDk​Decisioneke_kek​
001early (edge sample is still the old bit)+1+1+1
110early+1+1+1
011late (edge sample is already the new bit)−1-1−1
100late−1-1−1
0any0no transition000
1any1no transition000

(In logic this is the difference of two XORs: ek=(Ek⊕Dk)−(Dk−1⊕Ek)e_k=(E_k\oplus D_k)-(D_{k-1}\oplus E_k)ek​=(Ek​⊕Dk​)−(Dk−1​⊕Ek​). A timing diagram of the three samples is panel (a) of the figure in Numerical check below.)

Define the timing error Δt≡tdata−tclk\Delta t\equiv t_{\text{data}}-t_{\text{clk}}Δt≡tdata​−tclk​: the instant of the data transition minus the instant of the edge-sampling clock, positive when the clock is early. The truth table above is then

ek={sign(Δtk),data transition present0,no transitione_k=\begin{cases}\text{sign}(\Delta t_k), & \text{data transition present}\\ 0, & \text{no transition}\end{cases}ek​={sign(Δtk​),0,​data transition presentno transition​

Three key points:

  • The output is only ±1\pm1±1 (and 0): there is no information about "how large" the error is, only its direction. So it has no PD gain KPDK_{PD}KPD​ in the conventional sense (V/rad or 1/s) — exactly what Step 2 resolves.
  • Updates only on transitions: random NRZ data has transition density ρT≈0.5\rho_T\approx0.5ρT​≈0.5; during long runs of 0s or 1s the loop is "blind," one reason specifications require 8b/10b, 64b/66b or scrambling to bound the run length.
  • It is simultaneously the data sampler: DkD_kDk​ is the recovered data. So the CDR's lock target "clock aligned to the data edge" automatically equals "data sample at the eye center" — connecting directly to the JTOL margin UI−TJeye\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}UI−TJeye​ of Step 4.

Loop polarity: in the diagram ϕdata,ϕclk\phi_{data},\phi_{clk}ϕdata​,ϕclk​ are the time positions (delays, in s or UI) of the data transition and of the sampling-clock edge. Clock early (Δt=ϕdata−ϕclk>0\Delta t=\phi_{data}-\phi_{clk}\gt0Δt=ϕdata​−ϕclk​>0) → e=+1e=+1e=+1 → the phase code increases ϕclk\phi_{clk}ϕclk​ (moves the clock later) → Δt\Delta tΔt shrinks: negative feedback. With early/late swapped the same loop becomes positive feedback and locks to the eye edge instead of the eye center.

Step 2: linearization — Gaussian jitter smears sign into erf, gain K_bb = √(2/π)/σ_j​

Setup: the real Δt\Delta tΔt is not a constant but "nominal error Δt\Delta tΔt plus a zero-mean Gaussian term nnn," n∼N(0,σj2)n\sim\mathcal N(0,\sigma_j^2)n∼N(0,σj2​). This σj\sigma_jσj​ is the total rms jitter between the data edge and the sampling clock: the input data's RJ and the recovered clock's own jitter (the loop-shaped VCO σt\sigma_tσt​, the hunting of Step 3) are all included. The PD's expected output is:

⟨e⟩(Δt)=E[sign(Δt+n)]=P(n>−Δt)−P(n<−Δt)=2Φ ⁣(Δtσj)−1=erf⁡ ⁣(Δt2 σj),Φ(x)=12[1+erf⁡(x/2)].\begin{aligned} \langle e\rangle(\Delta t)&=E\big[\text{sign}(\Delta t+n)\big]=P(n>-\Delta t)-P(n<-\Delta t) =2\Phi\!\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\sigma_j}\right)-1 \\[4pt] &=\operatorname{erf}\!\left(\frac{\Delta t}{\sqrt2\,\sigma_j}\right), \qquad \Phi(x)=\tfrac12\Big[1+\operatorname{erf}\big(x/\sqrt2\big)\Big]. \end{aligned}⟨e⟩(Δt)​=E[sign(Δt+n)]=P(n>−Δt)−P(n<−Δt)=2Φ(σj​Δt​)−1=erf(2​σj​Δt​),Φ(x)=21​[1+erf(x/2​)].​

Step by step: (i) the expectation of sign is (+1)⋅P(positive)+(−1)⋅P(negative)(+1)\cdot P(\text{positive})+(-1)\cdot P(\text{negative})(+1)⋅P(positive)+(−1)⋅P(negative); (ii) the probability of n>−Δtn>-\Delta tn>−Δt is the Gaussian CDF Φ(Δt/σj)\Phi(\Delta t/\sigma_j)Φ(Δt/σj​); (iii) rewrite with the standard relation between Φ\PhiΦ and erf. The linearized gain is the slope of this curve at Δt=0\Delta t=0Δt=0:

 Kbb≡∂⟨e⟩∂Δt∣Δt=0=2π⋅12 σj=2π 1σj \boxed{\ K_{bb}\equiv\frac{\partial\langle e\rangle}{\partial\Delta t}\bigg|_{\Delta t=0} =\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}\cdot\frac{1}{\sqrt2\,\sigma_j}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\,\frac{1}{\sigma_j}\ } Kbb​≡∂Δt∂⟨e⟩​​Δt=0​=π​2​⋅2​σj​1​=π2​​σj​1​ ​

(Using ddxerf⁡(x)=2πe−x2\frac{d}{dx}\operatorname{erf}(x)=\frac{2}{\sqrt\pi}e^{-x^2}dxd​erf(x)=π␀␀​2​e−x2, which equals 2/π2/\sqrt\pi2/π​ at x=0x=0x=0, times the inner derivative 1/(2σj)1/(\sqrt2\sigma_j)1/(2​σj​).)

  • Dimension check: ⟨e⟩\langle e\rangle⟨e⟩ is dimensionless, Δt\Delta tΔt is in seconds → KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ has units s−1\text{s}^{-1}s−1 ✓. Multiplying by UI gives the dimensionless gain Kbb⋅UIK_{bb}\cdot\text{UI}Kbb​⋅UI ("output per UI of error").
  • Physical meaning: the larger σj\sigma_jσj​, the flatter the erf and the smaller the gain. The gain of a bang-bang loop is the reciprocal of the jitter — the central result of Lee–Kundert–Razavi (external literature, not among this site's five PDFs: J. Lee, K. S. Kundert, and B. Razavi, "Analysis and Modeling of Bang-Bang Clock and Data Recovery Circuits," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 39, no. 9, pp. 1571–1580, Sep. 2004).
  • Linear region: erf is approximately straight only for ∣Δt∣≲σj\lvert\Delta t\rvert\lesssim\sigma_j∣Δt∣≲σj​ (⟨e⟩(σj)=0.683\langle e\rangle(\sigma_j)=0.683⟨e⟩(σj​)=0.683, ⟨e⟩(2σj)=0.954\langle e\rangle(2\sigma_j)=0.954⟨e⟩(2σj​)=0.954 is already saturated); the tangent meets ±1\pm1±1 at Δt=±σjπ/2\Delta t=\pm\sigma_j\sqrt{\pi/2}Δt=±σj​π/2​. Larger errors enter the slew-limited region — where the −20-20−20 dB/dec JTOL segment of Step 4 lives.
  • Transition density: only transitions update the loop, so the average gain is further multiplied by ρT\rho_TρT​ (≈0.5\approx0.5≈0.5 for random data).

Worked example (site values): take the rms jitter between data edge and clock as this site's canonical example C, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs (free-running 5 GHz VCO, −100-100−100 dBc/Hz @ 1 MHz, integrated 1→100 MHz; used here as a representative σj\sigma_jσj​), UI =40=40=40 ps (25 Gb/s NRZ, as in final_exam problem 10).

Kbb=2π⋅1447.9×10−15 s=0.79794.479×10−13 s=1.78×1012 s−1,Kbb⋅UI=1.78×1012×40×10−12=71.3 (per UI).K_{bb}=\sqrt{\frac{2}{\pi}}\cdot\frac{1}{447.9\times10^{-15}\ \text{s}} =\frac{0.7979}{4.479\times10^{-13}\ \text{s}}=1.78\times10^{12}\ \text{s}^{-1}, \qquad K_{bb}\cdot\text{UI}=1.78\times10^{12}\times40\times10^{-12}=71.3\ \text{(per UI)}.Kbb​=π2​​⋅447.9×10−15 s1​=4.479×10−13 s0.7979​=1.78×1012 s−1,Kbb​⋅UI=1.78×1012×40×10−12=71.3 (per UI).

In other words the PD's expected output already hits ±1\pm1±1 when the clock is off by 1/71.3 UI=0.0141/71.3\ \text{UI}=0.0141/71.3 UI=0.014 UI =0.56=0.56=0.56 ps — the linear region is only half a picosecond wide. The smaller the σt\sigma_tσt​ the ISF gives (the cleaner the VCO), the larger KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ and the faster the loop — but the narrower the linear region: this is where bang-bang differs most from a linear PLL.

import numpy as np
from scipy.special import erf
sigma_t = 447.9e-15   # s, canonical example C (free-running VCO, 1-100 MHz)
UI = 40e-12           # s, 25 Gb/s NRZ
K_bb = np.sqrt(2/np.pi)/sigma_t
print(f"{K_bb:.3e}", round(K_bb*UI, 1))
# -> 1.781e+12 71.3
d = 1e-18             # numerical derivative of erf(dt/(sqrt2 sigma)) at 0
slope = (erf(d/(np.sqrt(2)*sigma_t)) - erf(-d/(np.sqrt(2)*sigma_t)))/(2*d)
print(f"{slope:.3e}", round(sigma_t*np.sqrt(np.pi/2)*1e12, 3))
# -> 1.781e+12 0.561

Step 3: the PI loop — φ[k+1] = φ[k] + K_p·sign(e), UI/2^b quantization, hunting limit cycle​

Most modern SerDes CDRs have no VCO in the loop: a shared PLL generates fixed-frequency multi-phase clocks, and the CDR uses a phase interpolator (PI) to interpolate the sampling clock between those phases. The PI is driven by a bbb-bit phase code; one UI is divided into 2b2^b2b steps:

ΔϕPI=UI2b(b=6: 40 ps64=0.625 ps=0.0156 UI).\Delta\phi_{PI}=\frac{\text{UI}}{2^b}\qquad(b=6:\ \frac{40\ \text{ps}}{64}=0.625\ \text{ps}=0.0156\ \text{UI}).ΔϕPI​=2bUI​(b=6: 6440 ps​=0.625 ps=0.0156 UI).

The simplest first-order bang-bang loop pushes the phase code one step in the direction the PD indicates every update period Tu=Ndec⋅UIT_u=N_{dec}\cdot\text{UI}Tu​=Ndec​⋅UI (NdecN_{dec}Ndec​ is the decimation/voting factor applied to the PD output):

ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kp sign(e[k]),Kp=m⋅ΔϕPI (m LSBs).\phi[k+1]=\phi[k]+K_p\,\text{sign}(e[k]),\qquad K_p=m\cdot\Delta\phi_{PI}\ (m\ \text{LSBs}).ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kp​sign(e[k]),Kp​=m⋅ΔϕPI​ (m LSBs).

Three consequences of discretization (external literature, not among this site's five PDFs: R. C. Walker, "Designing Bang-Bang PLLs for Clock and Data Recovery in Serial Data Transmission Systems," in Phase-Locking in High-Performance Systems, B. Razavi, Ed., IEEE Press, 2003):

  1. Hunting (limit cycle): once locked, the PD still only says "early" or "late," so the phase code hops back and forth around the optimum, producing a deterministic jitter of peak-to-peak KpK_pKp​; if the loop has a latency of DDD update periods (the pipeline between decision and execution), the phase overshoots by DDD extra steps before reversing and the limit cycle grows to peak-to-peak (2D+1)Kp(2D+1)K_p(2D+1)Kp​ (counted directly with the noise-free model in the Python below). This is a DJ: in the TJ budget it enters as DJpp\text{DJ}_{pp}DJpp​, added directly, not scaled with BER (see dj_dual_dirac).
  2. Quantization noise: treating the PI phase error as uniformly distributed, its rms is ΔϕPI/12=0.18\Delta\phi_{PI}/\sqrt{12}=0.18ΔϕPI​/12​=0.18 ps — the same order as σt=0.45\sigma_t=0.45σt​=0.45 ps, not negligible.
  3. Linearized bandwidth: substituting KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ from Step 2, the phase correction per update is ≈KpKbbρT Δt\approx K_p K_{bb}\rho_T\,\Delta t≈Kp​Kbb​ρT​Δt, and the continuous-time approximation gives a first-order loop
dϕclkdt≈KpKbbρTTu (ϕdata−ϕclk) ⇒ fBW≈KpKbbρTfu2π,fu=1Tu.\frac{d\phi_{clk}}{dt}\approx\frac{K_pK_{bb}\rho_T}{T_u}\,(\phi_{data}-\phi_{clk}) \ \Rightarrow\ f_{BW}\approx\frac{K_pK_{bb}\rho_T f_u}{2\pi},\qquad f_u=\frac{1}{T_u}.dtdϕclk​​≈Tu​Kp​Kbb​ρT​​(ϕdata​−ϕclk​) ⇒ fBW​≈2πKp​Kbb​ρT​fu​​,fu​=Tu​1​.
  • Dimension check: KpK_pKp​ [s] ×Kbb\times K_{bb}×Kbb​ [1/s] ×fu\times f_u×fu​ [1/s] === [1/s] ✓; KpKbbK_pK_{bb}Kp​Kbb​ is the (dimensionless) "loop gain per update"; the discrete loop needs KpKbbρT<2K_pK_{bb}\rho_T\lt2Kp​Kbb​ρT​<2 for stability, and the linearization itself holds only when Kp≲σjK_p\lesssim\sigma_jKp​≲σj​ (step smaller than the noise).
  • Worked (site values): Kp=1K_p=1Kp​=1 LSB =0.625=0.625=0.625 ps, Kbb=1.78×1012K_{bb}=1.78\times10^{12}Kbb​=1.78×1012 s−1^{-1}−1, ρT=0.5\rho_T=0.5ρT​=0.5. Ndec=1N_{dec}=1Ndec​=1 (update every UI): KpKbb=1.11K_pK_{bb}=1.11Kp​Kbb​=1.11 per update — already beyond what the linearization can describe (the 0.6250.6250.625 ps step exceeds σj=0.448\sigma_j=0.448σj​=0.448 ps), so the nominal fBW=2.2f_{BW}=2.2fBW​=2.2 GHz is meaningless; Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16 (fu=1.5625f_u=1.5625fu​=1.5625 GHz): fBW≈0.5×0.625 ps×1.78×1012 s−1×1.5625×109 s−1/2π=138f_{BW}\approx0.5\times0.625\text{ ps}\times1.78\times10^{12}\text{ s}^{-1} \times1.5625\times10^9\text{ s}^{-1}/2\pi=138fBW​≈0.5×0.625 ps×1.78×1012 s−1×1.5625×109 s−1/2π=138 MHz (0.55%0.55\%0.55% of the bit rate). This is the small-signal bandwidth of the proportional path, valid only inside the linear region (error ≲σj\lesssim\sigma_j≲σj​); it is not the type-II fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz template used to draw the mask in Steps 4–5 — the two differ by two orders of magnitude, and the slew line of Step 4 and the integral path of Step 5 explain how they are related. Honest statement: here Kp≈σjK_p\approx\sigma_jKp​≈σj​, so hunting pushes the effective σj\sigma_jσj​ up and KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ down; the Monte-Carlo of the "Numerical check" section below measures an effective gain per update of 0.380.380.38 (linearized 0.5570.5570.557) and an effective bandwidth of 949494 MHz.
  • Slew capability of the proportional path: at most (Kp/UI) fu(K_p/\text{UI})\,f_u(Kp​/UI)fu​ UI per second (the ceiling, reached when every update carries a decision), i.e. a trackable frequency offset of (Kp/UI) fu/fb(K_p/\text{UI})\,f_u/f_b(Kp​/UI)fu​/fb​: 1/64=15 6251/64=15\,6251/64=15625 ppm for Ndec=1N_{dec}=1Ndec​=1, 977977977 ppm for Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16. If, as in the linearized model above, each update uses only one PD decision, half of the updates of random data have no transition and do not move the phase, so the average slew is multiplied by ρT\rho_TρT​ (Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16: 488488488 ppm); a majority vote over the NdecN_{dec}Ndec​ decisions produces an output on almost every update and recovers 977977977 ppm. Step 5 compares this against the 5000 ppm of SSC.
import numpy as np
fb, UI, b = 25e9, 40e-12, 6
Kp = UI/2**b
print(round(Kp*1e12, 3), round(Kp/UI, 4), round(Kp/np.sqrt(12)*1e12, 3))
# -> 0.625 0.0156 0.18
K_bb = np.sqrt(2/np.pi)/447.9e-15
for Ndec in (1, 16):
    fu = fb/Ndec
    f_bw = 0.5*Kp*K_bb*fu/(2*np.pi)     # rho_T = 0.5 (random data); one sign per update, no voting
    print(Ndec, f"{f_bw:.3e}", f"{(Kp/UI)*fu/fb*1e6:.0f}")
# -> 1 2.215e+09 15625
# -> 16 1.384e+08 977
def hunting_pp(D, n=400):               # noise-free limit cycle, latency D updates, units of Kp
    phi, q, hist = 0.3, [0.0]*D, []
    for k in range(n):
        q.append(-np.sign(phi) if phi != 0 else 1.0)
        phi += q.pop(0)
        hist.append(phi)
    h = np.array(hist[n//2:])
    return float(h.max() - h.min())
print([hunting_pp(D) for D in (0, 1, 2, 4)])
# -> [1.0, 3.0, 5.0, 9.0]

Sidebar: why a DLL does not "accumulate" jitter (external literature, not among this site's five PDFs: J. G. Maneatis, "Low-Jitter Process-Independent DLL and PLL Based on Self-Biased Techniques," IEEE J. Solid-State Circuits, vol. 31, no. 11, pp. 1723–1732, Nov. 1996). The PI architecture above is really DLL (delay-locked loop) thinking: there is no oscillator in the loop, only "a delay relative to the reference clock." An oscillator's phase is the integral of its frequency, so white noise → phase random walk → σΔt=κΔt\sigma_{\Delta t}=\kappa\sqrt{\Delta t}σΔt​=κΔt​ ([P2] Eq.(8), p.792, see lc_vs_ring); a delay line's error is re-zeroed by the reference edge every cycle, so noise is added once and never accumulates. The price is that the output jitter inherits the reference clock's jitter directly (there is no high-pass to filter it) and there is no frequency degree of freedom — so "frequency tracking" in a PI-CDR relies entirely on the integral path of Step 5 accumulating the phase code digitally.

Step 4: JTOL(f) = (UI − TJ_eye)/|1 − H(f)| and the −40 / −20 dB/dec mask segments​

pll_noise_budget already separated jitter transfer (∣Hlp∣2\lvert H_{lp}\rvert^2∣Hlp​∣2) from jitter tolerance (set by the error transfer 1−Hlp=Hhp1-H_{lp}=H_{hp}1−Hlp​=Hhp​): only the part of the input jitter the CDR fails to track, ϕerr=(1−H)ϕdata\phi_{err}=(1-H)\phi_{data}ϕerr​=(1−H)ϕdata​, eats the eye. Given an eye margin UI−TJeye\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}UI−TJeye​, the tolerable single-tone sinusoidal input jitter is

 JTOLpp(f)=UI−TJeye∣1−H(f)∣ \boxed{\ \text{JTOL}_{pp}(f)=\frac{\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}}{\lvert1-H(f)\rvert}\ } JTOLpp​(f)=∣1−H(f)∣UI−TJeye​​ ​

⚠️ Convention flag (peak vs peak-to-peak, a factor of 2): industry JTOL masks are specified peak-to-peak (UI pp). With the sample at the eye center, it may deviate by (UI−TJeye)/2(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/2(UI−TJeye​)/2 either way, so a sinusoidal error of peak ≤(UI−TJeye)/2\le(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/2≤(UI−TJeye​)/2 ⇔ peak-to-peak ≤UI−TJeye\le\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}≤UI−TJeye​ — the formula above therefore matches the mask when read as peak-to-peak; pll_noise_budget calls the same expression a peak amplitude — same numbers, a 2× difference in reading, so say which one you mean when quoting it.

Where the three mask segments come from — approximate the type-II second-order 1−Hlp=Hhp(s)=s2s2+2ζωns+ωn21-H_{lp}=H_{hp}(s)=\dfrac{s^2}{s^2+2\zeta\omega_ns+\omega_n^2}1−Hlp​=Hhp​(s)=s2+2ζωn​s+ωn2​s2​ piecewise:

Band∣Hhp∣\lvert H_{hp}\rvert∣Hhp​∣ approximationJTOL slopePhysics
f≪fz=fn/(2ζ)f\ll f_z=f_n/(2\zeta)f≪fz​=fn​/(2ζ)(f/fn)2(f/f_n)^2(f/fn​)2−40-40−40 dB/decfrequency integrator + phase integrator: two integrators track slow excursions

A bang-bang loop adds one more slew-limited −20-20−20 dB/dec line: a sinusoidal phase of peak-to-peak AppA_{pp}App​ at frequency fff has maximum slope πAppf\pi A_{pp}fπApp​f, while the proportional path can move at most (Kp/UI)fu(K_p/\text{UI})f_u(Kp​/UI)fu​ UI per second, so

App≤(Kp/UI) fuπf(−20 dB/dec; Walker 2003, Lee–Kundert–Razavi 2004).A_{pp}\le\frac{(K_p/\text{UI})\,f_u}{\pi f}\qquad(-20\ \text{dB/dec; Walker 2003, Lee–Kundert–Razavi 2004}).App​≤πf(Kp​/UI)fu​​(−20 dB/dec; Walker 2003, Lee–Kundert–Razavi 2004).

This line belongs to a proportional-only loop. With the Step-3 numbers (Kp=0.625K_p=0.625Kp​=0.625 ps, Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16): (Kp/UI)fu=0.015625×1.5625×109=2.44×107(K_p/\text{UI})f_u=0.015625\times1.5625\times10^9=2.44\times10^7(Kp​/UI)fu​=0.015625×1.5625×109=2.44×107 UI/s, so at 30 kHz App≤2.44×107/(π×3×104)=259A_{pp}\le2.44\times10^7/(\pi\times3\times10^4)=259App​≤2.44×107/(π×3×104)=259 UI (halved to 129.5129.5129.5 UI with one decision per update and ρT=0.5\rho_T=0.5ρT​=0.5) — below the 521521521 UI that SSC demands in Step 5. In other words the first-order loop of Step 3 cannot follow SSC. The integral (frequency) path of Step 5 uses a frequency register to remember "how far to move per update", which removes this velocity limit and replaces it by an acceleration limit (−40-40−40 dB/dec, derived in Step 5); only with it does the −40-40−40 dB/dec segment in the first table row exist.

How the lines combine: the three linear segments are the three terms of 1/∣Hhp∣=∣1+2ζωn/s+ωn2/s2∣1/\lvert H_{hp}\rvert=\lvert1+2\zeta\omega_n/s+\omega_n^2/s^2\rvert1/∣Hhp​∣=∣1+2ζωn​/s+ωn2​/s2∣, and whichever term is largest dominates; the large-signal limits of a bang-bang loop (slew line, acceleration line) are a separate upper bound, so the actual tolerance is min⁡(linear value, large-signal limit)\min(\text{linear value},\ \text{large-signal limit})min(linear value, large-signal limit). This is why datasheet JTOL curves look the way they do: −40-40−40 at low frequency, −20-20−20 in the middle, a plateau at high frequency — each segment corresponds to a different mechanism in the loop.

Worked example (the linear template of the mask; site values, the same set as pll_noise_budget): UI =40=40=40 ps, σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs, TJeye=2Q−1(10−12)σt=2×7.03×0.4479\text{TJ}_{eye}=2Q^{-1}(10^{-12})\sigma_t=2\times7.03\times0.4479TJeye​=2Q−1(10−12)σt​=2×7.03×0.4479 ps =6.30=6.30=6.30 ps =0.157=0.157=0.157 UI, margin 0.8430.8430.843 UI; type-II, fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz, ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707.

JTOL(10 kHz)=0.843(104/106)2=0.84310−4=8.4×103 UI,JTOL(30 kHz)=0.8439.0×10−4=936 UI,JTOL(100 kHz)=84 UI,JTOL(1 MHz)=0.8430.707=1.19 UI,JTOL(10 MHz)=0.84 UI.\begin{aligned} \text{JTOL}(10\ \text{kHz})&=\frac{0.843}{(10^4/10^6)^2}=\frac{0.843}{10^{-4}}=8.4\times10^{3}\ \text{UI},\\ \text{JTOL}(30\ \text{kHz})&=\frac{0.843}{9.0\times10^{-4}}=936\ \text{UI},\quad \text{JTOL}(100\ \text{kHz})=84\ \text{UI},\quad \text{JTOL}(1\ \text{MHz})=\frac{0.843}{0.707}=1.19\ \text{UI},\quad \text{JTOL}(10\ \text{MHz})=0.84\ \text{UI}. \end{aligned}JTOL(10 kHz)JTOL(30 kHz)​=(104/106)20.843​=10−40.843​=8.4×103 UI,=9.0×10−40.843​=936 UI,JTOL(100 kHz)=84 UI,JTOL(1 MHz)=0.7070.843​=1.19 UI,JTOL(10 MHz)=0.84 UI.​

10 kHz→100 kHz is exactly −40-40−40 dB/dec (8426→84.38426\to84.38426→84.3, 100×100\times100×); with ζ=0.707\zeta=0.707ζ=0.707 the zero fz=707f_z=707fz​=707 kHz sits almost on fnf_nfn​, so no −20-20−20 segment is visible; raising ζ\zetaζ to 4 (fz=125f_z=125fz​=125 kHz) turns the 100 kHz→1 MHz slope into −24-24−24 dB/dec — one origin of the −20-20−20 dB/dec mid-segment in specifications.

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_highpass_mag2
UI, sigma_t, qinv = 40e-12, 447.9e-15, 7.03
TJ_eye = 2*qinv*sigma_t
margin_UI = 1 - TJ_eye/UI
print(round(TJ_eye*1e12, 2), round(TJ_eye/UI, 3), round(margin_UI, 3))
# -> 6.3 0.157 0.843
fn, zeta = 1e6, 0.707
for f in [1e4, 3e4, 1e5, 1e6, 1e7]:
    H_hp = np.sqrt(H_highpass_mag2(np.array([f]), fn, zeta)[0])   # amplitude |1-H_lp|
    print(f"{f:.0e}", f"{H_hp:.3e}", round(margin_UI/H_hp, 2))
# -> 1e+04 1.000e-04 8425.63
# -> 3e+04 9.000e-04 936.18
# -> 1e+05 1.000e-02 84.26
# -> 1e+06 7.072e-01 1.19
# -> 1e+07 1.000e+00 0.84
def jtol_slope(zeta, fa, fb):           # dB per decade of JTOL between fa and fb = 10 fa
    Ha, Hb = (np.sqrt(H_highpass_mag2(np.array([x]), fn, zeta)[0]) for x in (fa, fb))
    return float(20*np.log10((margin_UI/Hb)/(margin_UI/Ha)))
for zeta in (0.707, 4.0):
    print(zeta, [round(jtol_slope(zeta, fa, 10*fa), 1) for fa in (1e4, 1e5, 1e6)])
# -> 0.707 [-40.0, -37.0, -3.0]
# -> 4.0 [-37.9, -24.0, -16.0]
Kp, fu, rho_T = UI/64, 25e9/16, 0.5     # Step-3 loop: proportional path only
slew = (Kp/UI)*fu                       # UI/s when every update carries a decision
print(f"{slew:.3e}", round(slew/(np.pi*3e4), 1), round(rho_T*slew/(np.pi*3e4), 1), round(rho_T*slew/25e9*1e6))
# -> 2.441e+07 259.0 129.5 488

Step 5: SSC — the triangular FM the CDR must track, 521 UI peak-to-peak phase​

Spread-spectrum clocking (SSC) deliberately sweeps the transmitter clock frequency as a triangle wave at fm≈30f_m\approx30fm​≈30–333333 kHz from nominal down to −δ-\delta−δ (down-spread, PCIe-style δ=0.5%\delta=0.5\%δ=0.5%; PCI Express Base Specification, version to be verified; external literature, not among this site's five PDFs) to spread EMI energy. To the receiver's CDR this is not noise but a deterministic FM that must be tracked — especially when the RX reference clock is not spread along with it (separate-reference architectures).

Deriving the peak-to-peak phase step by step. Let the bit rate be fbf_bfb​; the frequency offset relative to the center value is a triangle wave of amplitude ±δfb/2\pm\delta f_b/2±δfb​/2 and period Tm=1/fmT_m=1/f_mTm​=1/fm​. The phase (in UI) is the integral of the frequency offset; the area of the triangle's positive half-period is 12⋅Tm2⋅δfb2=δfbTm8\tfrac12\cdot\tfrac{T_m}{2}\cdot\tfrac{\delta f_b}{2}=\dfrac{\delta f_bT_m}{8}21​⋅2Tm​​⋅2δfb​​=8δfb​Tm​​, which is the peak-to-peak phase:

 Δϕpp=δ fb Tm8 UI=14 Tm Δfpk cycles (Δfpk=δfclk/2 is the clock’s peak frequency deviation).\boxed{\ \Delta\phi_{pp}=\frac{\delta\,f_b\,T_m}{8}\ \text{UI} =\frac{1}{4}\,T_m\,\Delta f_{pk}\ \text{cycles}\ }\qquad(\Delta f_{pk}=\delta f_{clk}/2\ \text{is the clock's peak frequency deviation}). Δϕpp​=8δfb​Tm​​ UI=41​Tm​Δfpk​ cycles ​(Δfpk​=δfclk​/2 is the clock’s peak frequency deviation).

Substituting fb=25f_b=25fb​=25 Gb/s (half-rate clock fclk=12.5f_{clk}=12.5fclk​=12.5 GHz), δ=0.005\delta=0.005δ=0.005, fm=30f_m=30fm​=30 kHz (Tm=33.3T_m=33.3Tm​=33.3 µs):

Δfpk=0.005×12.5 GHz2=31.25 MHz,Δϕpp=14×33.3 μs×31.25 MHz=260 cycles=260×80 ps=20.8 ns=521 UI.\Delta f_{pk}=\frac{0.005\times12.5\ \text{GHz}}{2}=31.25\ \text{MHz},\quad \Delta\phi_{pp}=\tfrac14\times33.3\ \mu\text{s}\times31.25\ \text{MHz}=260\ \text{cycles} =260\times80\ \text{ps}=20.8\ \text{ns}=521\ \text{UI}.Δfpk​=20.005×12.5 GHz​=31.25 MHz,Δϕpp​=41​×33.3 μs×31.25 MHz=260 cycles=260×80 ps=20.8 ns=521 UI.
  • Dimension check: [s]×[1/s]=[\text{s}]\times[\text{1/s}]=[s]×[1/s]= dimensionless (a cycle count) ✓; one 12.5 GHz cycle =2=2=2 UI ✓.
  • This is a phase excursion of over five hundred UI, four orders of magnitude larger than any RJ. The tolerance at 30 kHz must exceed 521521521 UI, and the test must use the min⁡(linear value, large-signal limit)\min(\text{linear value},\ \text{large-signal limit})min(linear value, large-signal limit) of Step 4: the linear value of the type-II fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz template is 936936936 UI (8.4×1038.4\times10^38.4×103 UI at 10 kHz), but with the proportional path only the slew line gives just 259259259 UI ✗ — the 936936936 UI is reachable only with the integral path (last three bullets of this step).
  • How large is the residual error: each leg of the triangular FM is a frequency ramp = a phase parabola ϕin=12at2\phi_{in}=\tfrac12at^2ϕin​=21​at2 with a=δfb/(Tm/2)=7.5×1012a=\delta f_b/(T_m/2)=7.5\times10^{12}a=δfb​/(Tm​/2)=7.5×1012 UI/s². For a type-II second-order loop the final value of E(s)=Hhp(s)⋅a/s3E(s)=H_{hp}(s)\cdot a/s^3E(s)=Hhp​(s)⋅a/s3 is ess=a/ωn2=7.5×1012/(2π×106)2=0.19e_{ss}=a/\omega_n^2=7.5\times10^{12}/(2\pi\times10^6)^2=0.19ess​=a/ωn2​=7.5×1012/(2π×106)2=0.19 UI — the ramp reverses every Tm/2T_m/2Tm​/2, so the error is a square wave of ±0.19\pm0.19±0.19 UI (peak-to-peak 0.38 UI). Frequency-domain cross-check: the peak-to-peak fundamental of the piecewise-parabolic phase is not 521 UI but 521×32/π3=538521\times32/\pi^3=538521×32/π3=538 UI (the triangle wave's 8/π28/\pi^28/π2 fundamental, integrated once more); times ∣Hhp(30 kHz)∣=9.0×10−4\lvert H_{hp}(30\ \text{kHz})\rvert=9.0\times10^{-4}∣Hhp​(30 kHz)∣=9.0×10−4 this gives 0.480.480.48 UI pp =0.38×4/π=0.38\times4/\pi=0.38×4/π, exactly the fundamental of that square wave ✓. This 0.19 UI must be subtracted from the 0.843 UI margin — SSC is a non-trivial DJ item in the CDR budget. (Note that this is the result for the linear-PD template: a bang-bang PD saturates at ±0.56\pm0.56±0.56 ps, and an error of 0.190.190.19 UI would require an average output of Kbb⋅0.19 UI=13.5≫1K_{bb}\cdot0.19\ \text{UI}=13.5\gg1Kbb​⋅0.19 UI=13.5≫1, which cannot happen; the SSC residual of the bang-bang loop itself is in the last bullet.)
  • A first-order (type-I) loop fails: a first-order loop with the same 1 MHz bandwidth has ∣1−H∣=f/f2+fBW2=0.030\lvert1-H\rvert=f/\sqrt{f^2+f_{BW}^2}=0.030∣1−H∣=f/f2+fBW2​​=0.030 @30 kHz → JTOL of only 282828 UI ≪521\ll521≪521; more fundamentally, a type-I loop has a static phase error for a 5000 ppm frequency offset of Δf/(2πfBW)=0.005×25×109/(2π×106)=19.9\Delta f/(2\pi f_{BW})=0.005\times25\times10^9/(2\pi\times10^6)=19.9Δf/(2πfBW​)=0.005×25×109/(2π×106)=19.9 UI — it simply loses lock.
  • Who tracks it inside the bang-bang PI loop: Step 3 computed the proportional path's frequency-tracking ceiling of 977977977 ppm (Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16; 488488488 ppm with a single decision per update) <5000\lt5000<5000 ppm — equivalently the Step-4 slew line of 259259259 UI <521\lt521<521 UI — so the proportional path cannot follow SSC; tracking SSC is the job of the integral (frequency) path: ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kpsign(e)+ω[k]\phi[k+1]=\phi[k]+K_p\text{sign}(e)+\omega[k]ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kp​sign(e)+ω[k], ω[k+1]=ω[k]+Kisign(e)\omega[k+1]=\omega[k]+K_i\text{sign}(e)ω[k+1]=ω[k]+Ki​sign(e), where the frequency register ω\omegaω remembers "how many fractions of an LSB to advance per update," leaving the PD to handle only jitter. This is why digital CDRs are almost always type-II.
  • The integral path trades the velocity limit for an acceleration limit: ω\omegaω changes by at most KiK_iKi​ per update (ρTKi\rho_TK_iρT​Ki​ on average for random data), so the phase acceleration is bounded by amax=ρT(Ki/UI)fu2a_{max}=\rho_T(K_i/\text{UI})f_u^2amax​=ρT​(Ki​/UI)fu2​ (units: [UI/update²]×[update/s]² === UI/s² ✓). A sinusoidal phase of peak-to-peak AppA_{pp}App​ has maximum acceleration 2π2f2App2\pi^2f^2A_{pp}2π2f2App​, hence App≤amax/(2π2f2)A_{pp}\le a_{max}/(2\pi^2f^2)App​≤amax​/(2π2f2) (−40-40−40 dB/dec). Take Ki=Kp/1024=0.61K_i=K_p/1024=0.61Ki​=Kp​/1024=0.61 fs/update² (the Step-3 loop plus this integral path): amax=1.86×1013a_{max}=1.86\times10^{13}amax​=1.86×1013 UI/s². (i) The SSC ramp a=7.5×1012a=7.5\times10^{12}a=7.5×1012 UI/s² uses only 40%40\%40% of it ✓ (the minimum for tracking SSC is Ki>0.25K_i\gt0.25Ki​>0.25 fs/update²); (ii) the acceleration line at 30 kHz is 104810481048 UI >521\gt521>521 UI ✓; (iii) written in the low-frequency form of the template, (UI−TJeye) fn,eq2/f2(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})\,f_{n,eq}^2/f^2(UI−TJeye​)fn,eq2​/f2, it gives fn,eq=amax/(2π2×0.843)=1.06f_{n,eq}=\sqrt{a_{max}/(2\pi^2\times0.843)}=1.06fn,eq​=amax​/(2π2×0.843)​=1.06 MHz. This is how the Step-3 loop relates to the fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz template of Steps 4–5: the template is an equivalent way of writing this bang-bang loop's large-signal −40-40−40 dB/dec line (936936936 UI versus 104810481048 UI), not its small-signal transfer function — the small-signal loop has fn=5.8f_n=5.8fn​=5.8 MHz, ζ=11.9\zeta=11.9ζ=11.9 (proportional-path bandwidth 2ζfn=1382\zeta f_n=1382ζfn​=138 MHz) and a linear value of 3.2×1043.2\times10^43.2×104 UI at 30 kHz, so the acceleration line is what actually binds. Conversely, for the small-signal response itself to be 1 MHz / 0.707, KpK_pKp​ would have to shrink to 6.46.46.4 fs ≈\approx≈ LSB/98, and the slew line of that loop at 30 kHz would be only a few UI.
  • SSC residual of the bang-bang loop: while tracking a ramp the frequency register must change at the rate aaa, so the PD's average output must be ρTerf⁡(Δt/2σj)=ρT a/amax\rho_T\operatorname{erf}(\Delta t/\sqrt2\sigma_j)=\rho_T\,a/a_{max}ρT​erf(Δt/2​σj​)=ρT​a/amax​ and the mean error is Δt=2 σjerf⁡−1(a/amax)=0.24\Delta t=\sqrt2\,\sigma_j\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(a/a_{max})=0.24Δt=2​σj​erf−1(a/amax​)=0.24 ps (with σj\sigma_jσj​ alone; the simulation measures 0.380.380.38 ps once the hunting is folded into σj\sigma_jσj​) — picoseconds, not the 0.190.190.19 UI =7.6=7.6=7.6 ps of the linear template.
import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_highpass_mag2
fb, UI = 25e9, 40e-12         # bit rate, UI
delta, fm = 0.005, 30e3       # -0.5 % down-spread, 30 kHz triangle (PCIe-style)
Tm = 1/fm
pp_cycles = 0.25*Tm*(delta*12.5e9/2)   # half-rate 12.5 GHz clock: +-31.25 MHz around centre
pp_UI = delta*fb*Tm/8
print(round(pp_cycles, 1), round(pp_UI, 1))
# -> 260.4 520.8
fn, zeta = 1e6, 0.707
margin_UI = 1 - 2*7.03*447.9e-15/UI    # 0.843 UI eye margin (Step 4)
a = (delta*fb)/(Tm/2)                  # phase acceleration during each ramp, UI/s^2
e_ss = a/(2*np.pi*fn)**2
H30 = np.sqrt(H_highpass_mag2(np.array([fm]), fn, zeta)[0])
pp_fund = pp_UI*32/np.pi**3            # fundamental (pp) of the piecewise-parabolic phase, not its pp
print(round(pp_fund, 1), f"{a:.2e}", round(e_ss, 3), round(pp_fund*H30, 3), round(margin_UI/H30, 1))
# -> 537.5 7.50e+12 0.19 0.484 936.2
fbw1 = 1e6                             # first-order (type-I) loop with the same bandwidth
H1 = fm/np.sqrt(fm**2 + fbw1**2)
print(round(margin_UI/H1, 1), round(delta*fb/(2*np.pi*fbw1), 1))
# -> 28.1 19.9
from scipy.special import erfinv
Kp, fu, rho_T = UI/64, fb/16, 0.5      # Step-3 loop (N_dec = 16) plus an integral path
K_bb = np.sqrt(2/np.pi)/447.9e-15
Ki = Kp/1024                           # s per update^2
a_max = rho_T*(Ki/UI)*fu**2            # UI/s^2: acceleration limit of the frequency register
print(f"{Ki*1e15:.4f}", f"{a_max:.3e}", round(a/a_max, 3), round(a_max/(2*np.pi**2*fm**2), 1),
      round(a*UI/(rho_T*fu**2)*1e15, 3))
# -> 0.6104 1.863e+13 0.403 1048.5 0.246
fn_eq = np.sqrt(a_max/(2*np.pi**2*margin_UI))            # large-signal equivalent of the template
fn_ss = np.sqrt(Ki*K_bb*rho_T)*fu/(2*np.pi)              # small-signal natural frequency
zeta_ss = Kp*K_bb*rho_T/(2*np.sqrt(Ki*K_bb*rho_T))
H_ss = np.sqrt(H_highpass_mag2(np.array([fm]), fn_ss, zeta_ss)[0])
print(round(fn_eq/1e6, 3), round(fn_ss/1e6, 2), round(zeta_ss, 1), round(2*zeta_ss*fn_ss/1e6, 1),
      f"{margin_UI/H_ss:.2e}")
# -> 1.058 5.8 11.9 138.4 3.17e+04
Kp_lin = 2*zeta*2*np.pi*fn/(K_bb*rho_T*fu)               # K_p whose small-signal loop IS 1 MHz / 0.707
print(round(Kp_lin*1e15, 2), round(Kp/Kp_lin, 1), round((Kp_lin/UI)*fu/(np.pi*fm), 2),
      round(0.19*UI*K_bb, 1), round(np.sqrt(2)*447.9e-15*erfinv(a/a_max)*1e12, 3))
# -> 6.38 97.9 2.65 13.5 0.237

Numerical check: the Monte-Carlo and time-domain runs of lab_45​

Every formula of the five steps is a linearization or an asymptote; simulations/lab_45_bb_cdr.py checks each of them with a behavioural model. The model uses exactly this page's numbers: 25 Gb/s, UI =40=40=40 ps, σj=447.9\sigma_j=447.9σj​=447.9 fs, Kp=UI/64K_p=\text{UI}/64Kp​=UI/64, Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16 (fu=1.5625f_u=1.5625fu​=1.5625 GHz), one Alexander decision per update (ρT=0.5\rho_T=0.5ρT​=0.5), Ki=Kp/1024K_i=K_p/1024Ki​=Kp​/1024; the pass/fail criterion is "the peak of the deterministic tracking error ≤(UI−TJeye)/2\le(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/2≤(UI−TJeye​)/2", i.e. the 0.8430.8430.843 UI peak-to-peak margin of Step 4.

"PD 平均輸出 ⟨e⟩" = mean PD output ⟨e⟩; "(c) 一階 bang-bang 迴路的 hunting" = (c) hunting of the first-order bang-bang loop; "無雜訊，延遲 D=…：峰峰 … K_p" = noise-free, latency D=…: peak-to-peak … K_p; "有 jitter：rms …" = with jitter: rms …; "更新次數 k" = update index k; "時脈相位誤差 [K_p]" = clock phase error [K_p]; "(d) 正弦 jitter 容忍度：模擬 vs 三條線" = (d) sinusoidal jitter tolerance: simulation vs three lines; "線性 type-II 樣板" = linear type-II template; "slew 線" = slew line; "加速度線" = acceleration line; "平台" = plateau; "模擬：只有比例路徑" = simulation: proportional path only; "模擬：比例＋積分路徑" = simulation: proportional + integral path; "SSC 需求 521 UI @ 30 kHz" = SSC requirement 521 UI @ 30 kHz; "正弦 jitter 頻率 f [Hz]" = sinusoidal jitter frequency f [Hz]; "可容忍輸入 jitter [UI 峰峰]" = tolerable input jitter [UI peak-to-peak]; "(e) SSC（−0.5 %、30 kHz 三角）追蹤誤差" = (e) SSC (−0.5 %, 30 kHz triangle) tracking error; "只有比例路徑（失鎖）" = proportional path only (lock lost); "比例＋積分路徑" = proportional + integral path; "時間 [µs]" = time [µs]; "追蹤誤差 Δt [UI]（symlog）" = tracking error Δt [UI] (symlog); "(f) 積分路徑追 SSC：誤差只有 ps 等級" = (f) the integral path tracking SSC: the error is only picoseconds; "比例＋積分：誤差 [ps]" = proportional + integral: error [ps]; "區塊平均" = block average; "追蹤誤差 Δt [ps]" = tracking error Δt [ps]; "SSC 頻偏 [ppm]" = SSC frequency offset [ppm].

How to read the figure

  • (a) The three samples: the transition is at t=0t=0t=0. With the clock early (blue) all three samples shift left, EkE_kEk​ falls before the transition and reads the old bit (Ek=Dk−1E_k=D_{k-1}Ek​=Dk−1​); with the clock late (red) EkE_kEk​ falls after the transition and reads the new bit (Ek=DkE_k=D_kEk​=Dk​). This is the truth table of Step 1.
  • (b) PD characteristic: applying the truth table literally to random NRZ data (edges carrying Gaussian jitter σj\sigma_jσj​) and counting only bits with a transition, the slope at the origin is 0.99 Kbb0.99\,K_{bb}0.99Kbb​; averaged over all bits it is 0.49 Kbb0.49\,K_{bb}0.49Kbb​ — the transition density (measured 0.500.500.50) is the ρT\rho_TρT​ of the Step-3 fBWf_{BW}fBW​ formula.
  • (c) Hunting: without noise and with latency D=0,1,2D=0,1,2D=0,1,2 the limit cycle is exactly 1,3,51,3,51,3,5 KpK_pKp​ peak-to-peak ((2D+1)Kp(2D+1)K_p(2D+1)Kp​). With jitter it is no longer a tidy limit cycle but a noise-dithered random walk: the linearization gives σhunt=Kp/(2Kbb)=419\sigma_{hunt}=\sqrt{K_p/(2K_{bb})}=419σhunt​=Kp​/(2Kbb​)​=419 fs (from the variance recursion 2KpρTKbbσ2=Kp2ρT2K_p\rho_TK_{bb}\sigma^2=K_p^2\rho_T2Kp​ρT​Kbb​σ2=Kp2​ρT​, independent of ρT\rho_TρT​), the simulation measures 509509509 fs (ratio 1.221.221.22). The gap is exactly the honest statement of Step 3: with Kp≈σjK_p\approx\sigma_jKp​≈σj​ the erf has already bent, the effective gain per update is only 0.380.380.38 (linearized 0.5570.5570.557) and the effective bandwidth is 949494 MHz rather than 138138138 MHz.
  • (d) Sinusoidal jitter tolerance: the proportional-only loop (blue squares) hugs the slew line; at 30 kHz it measures 126126126 UI, 0.970.970.97 of the ρT\rho_TρT​ slew line of 129.5129.5129.5 UI (slightly lower because the random number of transitions makes the slewing itself fluctuate, so the loop needs some headroom); with a majority vote over 16 decisions it measures 262262262 UI, 1.011.011.01 of the 259259259 UI line. Both are below the purple star at 521521521 UI. With the integral path added (red circles) the low-frequency points follow the acceleration line: 972972972 UI at 30 kHz (0.930.930.93 of the 104810481048 UI acceleration line; linear template 936936936 UI), the mid-band returns to the slew line and the high band is the plateau — the three segments are acceleration, slew and static margin.
  • The plateau of (d) is below 0.843 UI: 0.540.540.54 UI is measured at 100 MHz. A large high-frequency sinusoidal jitter drives the PD into saturation and lowers its effective gain, so the recovered clock itself acquires an extra slow wander that eats part of the margin; the formula's UI−TJeye\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}UI−TJeye​ is the upper bound without that wander.
  • (e)(f) SSC: the proportional-only loop loses lock on the first ramp and the error accumulates to about 5.9×1035.9\times10^35.9×103 UI; with the integral path the peak error is 0.080.080.08 UI (3.13.13.1 ps) and the mean error on the ramps is 0.380.380.38 ps, changing sign when the ramp reverses — consistent with the Step-5 prediction 2σerf⁡−1(a/amax)\sqrt2\sigma\operatorname{erf}^{-1}(a/a_{max})2​σerf−1(a/amax​) (with σ\sigmaσ the effective value including hunting).
import numpy as np
from simulations.lab_45_bb_cdr import (alexander_mc, limit_cycle, hunting_noisy, sj_tolerance, bb_loop,
    ssc_phase, KP, KP_UI, KI_UI, K_BB, SIGMA_J, RHO_T, FU, UI, MARGIN_UI, N_DEC)
rng = np.random.default_rng(45)
d0 = 0.1*SIGMA_J                       # (b) literal Alexander truth table on random NRZ data
(ap, tp, rho), (am, tm, _) = alexander_mc(+d0, 4_000_000, rng), alexander_mc(-d0, 4_000_000, rng)
print(round((tp - tm)/(2*d0)/K_BB, 2), round((ap - am)/(2*d0)/K_BB, 2), round(rho, 2))
# -> 0.99 0.49 0.5
phi = hunting_noisy(1_000_000, rng)[5000:]          # (c) first-order loop, sigma_j present
g_eff = KP**2*RHO_T/(2*phi.var())
print([float(np.ptp(limit_cycle(D)[200:])) for D in (0, 1, 2)], round(phi.std()*1e15),
      round(np.sqrt(KP/(2*K_BB))*1e15), round(g_eff, 2), round(g_eff*FU/(2*np.pi)/1e6))
# -> [1.0, 3.0, 5.0] 509 419 0.38 94
f = 30e3                                            # (d) sinusoidal-jitter tolerance at 30 kHz, UI pp
s1, sv = RHO_T*KP_UI*FU/(np.pi*f), KP_UI*FU/(np.pi*f)
acc = RHO_T*KI_UI*FU**2/(2*np.pi**2*f**2)
j1 = sj_tolerance(f, 0.0, s1 + MARGIN_UI, rng, n_amp=64, span=0.2)
jv = sj_tolerance(f, 0.0, sv + MARGIN_UI, rng, vote=N_DEC, n_amp=64, span=0.2)
j2 = sj_tolerance(f, KI_UI, acc + MARGIN_UI, rng, n_amp=64, span=0.3)
jh = sj_tolerance(1e8, 0.0, MARGIN_UI, rng, n_amp=64, span=0.3)   # far above the loop bandwidth
print(round(j1), round(j1/s1, 2), round(jv), round(jv/sv, 2), round(j2), round(j2/acc, 2), round(jh, 2))
# -> 126 0.97 262 1.01 972 0.93 0.54
n, per = int(3*FU/f), int(FU/f)                     # (e) SSC: -0.5 %, 30 kHz triangle, 3 periods
worst, tr = bb_loop(lambda k: np.repeat(ssc_phase(k)[:, None], 2, axis=1), n, 2,
                    np.array([0.0, KI_UI]), rng, eval_from=0, trace=True)
tau = np.mod(np.arange(n), per)/per                 # 0.15-0.45: settled part of the up-ramp
up = (tau > 0.15) & (tau < 0.45) & (np.arange(n) > per)
print(round(worst[0]), round(worst[1], 2), round(worst[1]*UI*1e12, 1), round(tr[up, 1].mean()*UI*1e12, 2))
# -> 5927 0.08 3.1 0.38

(The full script additionally sweeps 13 frequencies from 10 kHz to 100 MHz and draws the figure above; its random sequence differs, so its numbers differ from those above within Monte-Carlo scatter, e.g. 985985985 UI for the proportional+integral loop at 30 kHz.)

Limitations (honest statement)

  • This is a phase-domain behavioural model, not transistor level: ideal PI (no INL/DNL), no sampler metastability, no ISI, and the random jitter is only white Gaussian σj\sigma_jσj​, independent from update to update.
  • Tolerance is judged by "peak tracking error not exceeding (UI−TJeye)/2(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/2(UI−TJeye​)/2", not by actually counting a 10−1210^{-12}10−12 BER; each frequency point runs only 3 jitter periods (at least 3×1043\times10^43×104 updates) on an amplitude grid of about 3%3\%3%, and the high-frequency plateau value drops slightly with longer observation.
  • The JTOL and SSC experiments use loop latency D=0D=0D=0; real pipeline latency enlarges the hunting ((2D+1)Kp(2D+1)K_p(2D+1)Kp​) and reduces the usable KiK_iKi​.
  • The majority vote is checked only at the single 30 kHz point for the slew ceiling; its small-signal gain is not ρTKbb\rho_TK_{bb}ρT​Kbb​ and is not analysed on this page.
  • SSC is an ideal −0.5%-0.5\%−0.5% triangle starting at zero frequency offset; frequency acquisition is not simulated.

Every quantity in the five steps above is a function of σj\sigma_jσj​, bbb and NdecN_{dec}Ndec​; the widget below wires them together so that you can move one knob at a time and watch three plots and six readout cards:

PD characteristic: ⟨e⟩=erf⁡(Δt/2σj)\langle e\rangle=\operatorname{erf}(\Delta t/\sqrt2\sigma_j)⟨e⟩=erf(Δt/2​σj​) with the tangent KbbΔtK_{bb}\Delta tKbb​Δt at the origin (green dashed, reaching ±1\pm1±1 at ±σjπ/2\pm\sigma_j\sqrt{\pi/2}±σj​π/2​). The horizontal axis is fixed at ±3\pm3±3 ps, so the curve really steepens or flattens as you change σj\sigma_jσj​; the small red block is the width of one PI step KpK_pKp​.
  2. Time-domain hunting: the behavioural model of this page's numerical check (one Alexander decision per update, ρT=0.5\rho_T=0.5ρT​=0.5, fixed seed, latency D=0D=0D=0) with the sinusoidal jitter you choose on top, drawn as the 200 updates around the largest error of the run. The band is KpK_pKp​ wide; the yellow dashed lines are ±(UI−TJeye)/2\pm(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/2±(UI−TJeye​)/2.

Formulas (all from this page): K_bb = √(2/π)/σ_j (Step 2); K_p = UI/2^b, f_u = f_b/N_dec, f_BW = ρ_T K_p K_bb f_u/2π and the (2D+1)K_p hunting limit cycle (Step 3, D = 0 here; σ_hunt = √(K_p/2K_bb) is the linearised rms from the Numerical-check section); margin = UI − TJ_eye with TJ_eye = 2·7.03·σ_j (Step 4); slew line ρ_T(K_p/UI)f_u/(πf) and acceleration line ρ_T(K_i/UI)f_u²/(2π²f²) with K_i = K_p/1024 (Steps 4–5). The tolerance drawn is min(linear, max(large-signal lines, margin)): the linear curve is the first-order |1−H| for P only, or the type-II one with f_n = √(K_iK_bbρ_T)·f_u/2π and ζ = K_pK_bbρ_T/(2√(K_iK_bbρ_T)) for P + I; the large-signal lines are the Step 4–5 limits, and the margin is the floor that remains when the loop cannot follow at all. SSC tracking: with the integral path a_ssc = δ·f_b/(T_m/2) = 7.5×10¹² UI/s² must not exceed a_max; proportional only, the slew rate must exceed the 5000 ppm peak frequency offset. Panel (2) is the page's own behavioural model (one Alexander decision per update, ρ_T = 0.5, white Gaussian σ_j, ideal PI, latency D = 0, fixed seed 45), started with a raised-cosine ramp of the sinusoid, and shows the 200 updates around the largest error; its peak error is judged against (UI − TJ_eye)/2, as in the lab. Limits: pedagogical behavioural model, not transistor level; the linearised numbers are optimistic once K_p exceeds σ_j; near the pass/fail boundary the simulated verdict can differ from the analytic curve by the few-percent scatter seen in the lab (measured/line ≈ 0.93–1.01 on the page).

Things to try

  • Reconcile the defaults: at σj=447.9\sigma_j=447.9σj​=447.9 fs, Kbb=1.781×1012K_{bb}=1.781\times10^{12}Kbb​=1.781×1012 s−1^{-1}−1, 71.371.371.3 per UI; the 6-bit PI gives Kp=0.625K_p=0.625Kp​=0.625 ps; Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16 gives fBW=138.4f_{BW}=138.4fBW​=138.4 MHz; the linearized hunting rms is 419419419 fs; the 30 kHz JTOL is the acceleration line, 104810481048 UI; and a/amax=0.403a/a_{max}=0.403a/amax​=0.403 — all consistent with Steps 2–5.
  • Switch the integral path off: the 30 kHz JTOL drops to the slew line, 129.5129.5129.5 UI, the SSC card turns to "no" (488488488 ppm against 500050005000 ppm), the operating point turns from a dot into a cross, and the time-domain error runs away.
  • Push the PI bits towards 4: KpK_pKp​ grows and Kp/σjK_p/\sigma_jKp​/σj​ rises further above 1 (the default 6 bits is already above 1, so the warning line is there from the start) — the erf has bent and the linearized KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ and fBWf_{BW}fBW​ are optimistic; in the time-domain plot the band (KpK_pKp​ wide) becomes wider than the noise and the hunting turns into a deterministic back-and-forth. Towards 8 bits KpK_pKp​ shrinks below the noise, the warning disappears and the band sinks into the jitter.
  • Push NdecN_{dec}Ndec​ towards 1: fuf_ufu​ grows, and fBWf_{BW}fBW​ and the slew line rise in proportion (fBW=2.2f_{BW}=2.2fBW​=2.2 GHz at Ndec=1N_{dec}=1Ndec​=1 is the nominal value Step 3 calls meaningless); towards 64 both fall in proportion and the JTOL and SSC cards flip to failure.
  • Increase σj\sigma_jσj​: KbbK_{bb}Kbb​ falls, the PD curve flattens and its linear range widens; but TJeye=2×7.03 σj\text{TJ}_{eye}=2\times7.03\,\sigma_jTJeye​=2×7.03σj​ eats the margin and the high-frequency plateau drops. That is "the σt\sigma_tσt​ computed from the ISF sets both the gain and the margin".

Limitations: the tolerance curve is an analytic model and the time-domain panel is a behavioural simulation; near the pass/fail boundary they can differ by a few percent (the lab measured 0.930.930.93–1.011.011.01 times the lines). The simulation length is capped (600000 updates), so at low frequency or very small NdecN_{dec}Ndec​ it covers less than one jitter period, which the panel states; the other assumptions are those of the limitations list above (ideal PI, no ISI, white Gaussian σj\sigma_jσj​, D=0D=0D=0).

The eye margin UI−TJeye=1−2×7.03×0.300/40=0.8945\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye}=1-2\times7.03\times0.300/40=0.8945UI−TJeye​=1−2×7.03×0.300/40=0.8945 UI is far below both lines; the linear small-signal value (fn=10.02f_n=10.02fn​=10.02 MHz, ζ=10.3\zeta=10.3ζ=10.3) is 117211721172 UI, also far above the large-signal lines, so JTOL=max⁡(12.95, 20.97, 0.8945)=20.97\text{JTOL}=\max(12.95,\ 20.97,\ 0.8945)=20.97JTOL=max(12.95, 20.97, 0.8945)=20.97 UI peak-to-peak (the acceleration line dominates).

Dimension check: [UI/s]/[1/s]=[UI][\text{UI/s}]/[\text{1/s}]=[\text{UI}][UI/s]/[1/s]=[UI] and [UI/s2]/[1/s2]=[UI][\text{UI/s}^2]/[\text{1/s}^2]=[\text{UI}][UI/s2]/[1/s2]=[UI] ✓.

import numpy as np
from simulations.common.pll_utils import H_highpass_mag2
fb, UI, rho_T, qinv = 25e9, 40e-12, 0.5, 7.03
sigma, b, Ndec, f = 0.300e-12, 7, 8, 300e3       # quiz setting: P + I with K_i = K_p/1024
Kp = UI/2**b
fu = fb/Ndec
K_bb = np.sqrt(2/np.pi)/sigma
print(round(Kp*1e12, 4), f"{fu:.4e}", f"{K_bb:.3e}", round(K_bb*UI, 1))
# -> 0.3125 3.1250e+09 2.660e+12 106.4
margin = 1 - 2*qinv*sigma/UI
slew = rho_T*(Kp/UI)*fu/(np.pi*f)                 # UI pp, proportional path
acc = rho_T*(Kp/1024/UI)*fu**2/(2*np.pi**2*f**2)  # UI pp, integral path
print(round(margin, 4), round(slew, 2), round(acc, 2))
# -> 0.8945 12.95 20.97
g_p, g_i = Kp*K_bb*rho_T, Kp/1024*K_bb*rho_T      # small-signal gains per update
fn, zeta = np.sqrt(g_i)*fu/(2*np.pi), g_p/(2*np.sqrt(g_i))
lin = margin/np.sqrt(H_highpass_mag2(np.array([f]), fn, zeta)[0])
print(round(fn/1e6, 2), round(zeta, 2), round(lin))
# -> 10.02 10.31 1172
print(round(max(slew, acc, margin), 2), round(min(lin, max(slew, acc, margin)), 2))
# -> 20.97 20.97

Key takeaways​

  • The Alexander PD outputs only sign(Δt)\text{sign}(\Delta t)sign(Δt) (when a transition exists); Gaussian jitter smears it into ⟨e⟩=erf⁡(Δt/2σj)\langle e\rangle=\operatorname{erf}(\Delta t/\sqrt2\sigma_j)⟨e⟩=erf(Δt/2​σj​) with linearized gain Kbb=2/π/σjK_{bb}=\sqrt{2/\pi}/\sigma_jKbb​=2/π​/σj​.
  • Site values: σt=447.9\sigma_t=447.9σt​=447.9 fs → Kbb=1.78×1012K_{bb}=1.78\times10^{12}Kbb​=1.78×1012 s−1=71.3^{-1}=71.3−1=71.3/UI; the linear region is only ±0.56\pm0.56±0.56 ps. The σt\sigma_t␀σt​ computed from the ISF sets the gain and bandwidth of a bang-bang CDR.
  • PI: UI/2b\text{UI}/2^bUI/2b (6-bit → 0.625 ps); first-order BB update ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kpsign(e)\phi[k+1]=\phi[k]+K_p\text{sign}(e)ϕ[k+1]=ϕ[k]+Kp​sign(e); hunting peak-to-peak (2D+1)Kp(2D+1)K_p(2D+1)Kp​ is a DJ; linearized fBW=KpKbbρTfu/2πf_{BW}=K_pK_{bb}\rho_Tf_u/2\pifBW​=Kp​Kbb​ρT​fu​/2π (Ndec=16N_{dec}=16Ndec​=16 → 138 MHz small-signal for the proportional path; Monte-Carlo effective value 94 MHz).
  • JTOLpp(f)=(UI−TJeye)/∣1−H(f)∣\text{JTOL}_{pp}(f)=(\text{UI}-\text{TJ}_{eye})/\lvert1-H(f)\rvertJTOLpp​(f)=(UI−TJeye​)/∣1−H(f)∣: −40-40−40 (two integrators) / −20-20−20 (zero, or slew: App≤(Kp/UI)fu/πfA_{pp}\le(K_p/\text{UI})f_u/\pi fApp​≤(Kp​/UI)fu​/πf) / plateau. Site values: 6.306.306.30 ps =0.157=0.157=0.157 UI → 84/1.19/0.8484/1.19/0.8484/1.19/0.84 UI @ 100 kHz/1 MHz/10 MHz.
  • SSC (−0.5%-0.5\%−0.5%, 30 kHz, 25 Gb/s): Δϕpp=δfbTm/8=521\Delta\phi_{pp}=\delta f_bT_m/8=521Δϕpp​=δfb​Tm​/8=521 UI (260 cycles of the 12.5 GHz clock); the linear type-II fn=1f_n=1fn​=1 MHz template leaves ±0.19\pm0.19±0.19 UI, JTOL(30 kHz)=936=936=936 UI; first-order loop 28 UI and a 19.9 UI static error ✗.
  • With the proportional path only, the Step-3 bang-bang loop has a slew line of just 259259259 UI at 30 kHz (129.5129.5129.5 UI with a single decision) <521\lt521<521 UI ✗; adding the integral path (Ki=Kp/1024K_i=K_p/1024Ki​=Kp​/1024) replaces it by the acceleration line, 104810481048 UI ✓, equivalent to a template with fn≈1f_n\approx1fn​≈1 MHz — the 936936936 UI is reachable only through the integral path. Simulation: 126126126 / 262262262 / 972972972 UI.
  • DLL/PI has no oscillator → jitter does not accumulate (Maneatis 1996), but it neither filters the reference nor tracks frequency — frequency tracking relies on the integral path.
